How to keep cool in a heatwave: 25 tips from the people who know best, from a Rio lifeguard to an Egyptian archaeologist
For some, scorching days and humid nights are just the norm. So how do they stay chilled and comfortable?
Get up and out
Luis Pacherrez Antón is president of Agroperu Cooperative, a democratic collective of 102 small-scale farmers in the Chira River valley, Peru. He is based in Piura, known as “the city of eternal heat” because it stays hot and dry all year round. “The sun rays start to shine very early – from 9am,” he says. “So as people who work in cultivation, under a burning sun, we stay comfortable by starting much earlier and consuming the healthy foods that we produce, like bananas, oranges, lemons, grapes, papayas and avocados.”
Obada Almaitah, a diving instructor and course director in Aqaba, Jordan, says that summer temperatures regularly reach 40C, and can exceed that during heatwaves. “The sun is very strong, humidity is generally low and UV levels are high for much of the year, so I schedule physically demanding tasks during the early morning whenever possible.” When temperatures soar, flip your schedule to do chores before work – and forgo that weekend lie-in; instead, mow the lawn or lug shopping home first thing.
Tour guide Despina Savvidou has been leading visitors around the Acropolis of Athens for 48 years. She has witnessed first-hand the difference climate breakdown has made. “It’s like I’m in another country,” she says. “Thirty or 40 years ago, 32C was very hot; now 32C is normal. Two years ago, we had a heatwave that lasted two weeks.” Savvidou advises people to book on to her earliest tour – before the Acropolis even opens. “We have a tour that begins at 7.45am. We give a short introduction, and as soon as the doors open we go in. Between 8am and 10am – even if it’s 40C – it’s OK.”
Don’t wait until you’re thirsty to drink
This is a common tip from people who work in the baking sun, like Egyptian archaeologist Dr Zahi Hawass, who has worked at sites in the Nile delta, the Western desert and the Upper Nile valley. “The weather in Egypt during the summer is extremely hot, especially at archaeological sites such as Saqqara,” he says. “I make sure to drink water regularly while working outdoors. In the heat, it’s important not to wait until you feel very thirsty, but to keep drinking throughout the day.”
Sherene M El-Sioufi, a doctor in pulmonary and sleep medicine, lives and works in Jeddah, which experiences some of the hottest and most humid conditions in the world. She says: “In Saudi Arabia, many people drink laban, a yoghurt-based drink that provides hydration and electrolytes. The key is to drink consistently.”
Sip, don’t guzzle
“We tell people to drink little by little: at 10am take two sips, at 10.15am two more,” says Savvidou. “I have at least 15 glasses of water a day, but slowly.” Luiz Eduardo Dos Santos Nascimento, a lifeguard in Rio de Janeiro, where temperatures can exceed 40C during heatwaves, says: “I always keep a water bottle nearby and stay constantly hydrated during my shift.” John Napolo, a wildlife protection services manager at Etosha Heights Wildlife Monitoring Unit in Namibia, where summer temperatures can exceed 40C, says: “Each ranger carries five litres of water for the day. We drink three or four and pour the remainder on our heads when the heat is too much.”
Tip water on your head
Speaking of which, Prof Ollie Jay,director of the Heat and Health Research Centre at the University of Sydney, recommends this approach to cool down quickly: “When you apply water to the skin it evaporates, which cools you down, because it does the same job as sweating, but without the physiological stress of having to sweat. If you drink half your water and tip the other half over yourself, you get much more effective cooling.”
Dr Youssouf Moussa of the International Organization for Migration in Obock, Djibouti oversees humanitarian operations in a region facing extreme heat – in the week we speak a heat alert warns that temperatures could reach 53C. He uses “practical methods such as lightly wetting clothes, which helps cooling through evaporation”. To quickly cool an adult or child so they are comfortable enough to sleep, El-Sioufi suggests “a cool damp cloth on the neck, wrists or forehead”.
… Or ice your neck
Wondered why tennis players sit with ice towels around their necks? Jay and his team came up with an extreme heat policy for Tennis Australia. “Our studies showed that ice towels cool a relatively large area of the body in a small window, as a player spends just 80 seconds sitting in their chair.” Simply wrap crushed ice cubes in a rolled up wet towel and place it around your neck.
Take warm showers
For a speedy refresh, Savvidou swears by “a warm shower – no Greek person has a cold shower and most of us get under the water two or three times a day. I shower at 10am, again at 4pm, just to refresh without soap, and again before bed.” El-Sioufi also advises taking a shower before bed – a lukewarm one. “Many people assume a cold shower is best, but a lukewarm shower allows the body to cool gradually.” Michael Haindongo, a guide at Etosha Heights, who patrols this Namibian wildlife reserve daily, walking up to 500km (311 miles) a month and living in a camp in the bush for three-month rotations, takes a bedtime lukewarm shower, and when the temperature soars: “I wet a large towel and lie on it, and keep windows and doors open if there’s no threat from animals.”
He describes how houses in his village are naturally ventilated as they are thatched with grass and walls are made from wood, which is “semi open”. He also says “the Ovahimba people apply red ochre on their faces and any body parts exposed to the sun”. This natural cosmetic, made from butterfat and red ochre, provides protection against UV rays, thanks to high iron oxide content.
… Or play in a bucket
The village of Lytton in British Columbia became the hottest place ever in Canada for three days running in June 2021, reaching 49.6C. Dr Michael Schwandt is a medical health officer in the region. He says that to quickly cool small children, “one of the best things is immersion. It doesn’t need to be total, just getting their legs into a bathtub – or even a bucket. Similarly, placing cool, damp cloths on the body can help it to evaporate heat. That could be a flannel, a muslin or a lightly damp T-shirt – it shouldn’t have to be freezing cold, just cool.”
Down tools at peak times
“For humanitarian teams, rest is essential to stay safe and effective when working outside for extended periods in extreme heat,” says Moussa. “From noon until 3pm we limit movements to what is strictly necessary, although in case of an emergency, we remain fully available.” Haindongo isn’t “too sure if there’s such a thing as feeling comfortable working in the heat – we tolerate it, and would rather work early mornings and afternoons, or if necessary by moonlight.”
Federica Salvo, who runs the Giardino della Kolymbethra garden in Sicily, notes a similar approach: “Sicily holds the record for the highest temperature ever recorded in continental Europe – 48.8C on 11 August 2021.” She describes how Sicilians felt “overwhelmed” during that heatwave. “It was hard to work, or to concentrate on anything.” Fortunately, there are rules in place to protect people. “Throughout summer, work is prohibited from 12.30pm to 4pm in the construction and agriculture sectors, and during working hours workers are encouraged to take long breaks in the shade.”
Eat light, a little later
“If you have a big dinner, you suffer – you sweat and you don’t sleep,” says Savvidou. “On a hot day, for dinner I’ll have apricots, cherries and banana in yoghurt with raisins. For lunch, we cook vegetables – green beans, okra, peppers, aubergine – in olive oil with feta cheese and serve it with a big salad. In Greece, there is no meal without a salad. For lunch today, I grilled fish and served it with a salad of cucumber and tomatoes, and that’s it – no potatoes, no rice, no pasta.”
Carmen Vallejo Carmona, a grandmother in Seville – known as the frying pan of Spain thanks to sweltering summer temperatures – says her hot weather diet is “based around salads and cold dishes. The gazpacho in our town is more liquid, drunk from a glass. We also eat salmorejo (another chilled Andalucían soup), boquerones en vinagre (marinated anchovies), vegetables and the occasional ice-cream. Lunch is late – normally between 2pm and 3pm – and dinner is after 9pm, once the worst of the heat is gone.”
Moussa says: “In extreme heat we avoid heavy meals, especially at midday. Instead, we focus on light, water-rich foods and drink plenty of fluids, including tea. A typical breakfast includes lahooh, a soft flatbread, with tea and water. On the coast near Obock, Red Sea fish grilled Yemeni-style is very common.”
Eat to hydrate, too
Dr Rashmi Sarkar is a dermatologist in New Delhi, where summer daytime temperatures commonly reach 42-45C. She says: “Traditional Indian diets include many foods considered to be cooling and hydrating: yoghurt, chaas [buttermilk], coconut water, fresh fruits such as watermelon and mangoes, and cucumbers. Drinks such as lemon water, jaljeera [a spiced beverage], aam panna made from raw mango, [cordials such as] khus and sattu are popular because they help replace fluids and electrolytes.”
Almaitah says: “During long diving days, I replace electrolytes naturally through foods such as melon, cucumbers, tomatoes and yoghurt.” Nascimento notes that “it’s common in Rio for people to consume coconut water, natural juices and chilled fruit”; while Napolo says: “Some rangers have traditional knowledge of plant roots and tubers that can give you extra water.” If you want a root veg with a high water content for salads, radish is 95% water, while celeriac, carrot and beetroot are all 88%.
Remember, less isn’t always more
“One of the biggest misconceptions is that less clothing is better,” says El-Sioufi. “Many traditional practices – including wearing loose, flowing garments – evolved for a reason. They provide excellent protection from direct sunlight while allowing air circulation.” Napolo agrees: “The best way to stay cool is to be completely covered – long sleeves and trousers, and something to cover your face. The key is to have light, loose layers that allow airflow as you move.” Savvidou opts for cotton trousers that “are so wide you don’t know where the leg is, a loose shirt, and no belts. People think they need everything open in the heat, but this isn’t wise because you get dehydrated.”
Duong and Van, Vietnamese grandparents who live in Nam Dinh, where it’s very hot and humid, also cover up. “At home we wear shorts, loose dresses, vests, and men are topless, but when travelling by motorbike, people wear a full outfit on top of their normal clothes that covers their whole body, face and hands. It’s made of cotton.” Moussa also opts for light, loose, breathable clothing that protects the skin while allowing air to circulate. “In Djibouti, traditional clothing is well adapted to the heat. Women often wear pygama, a long, loose, lightweight dress, while men wear the futa, a cotton wrap that allows airflow.”
Don’t forget accessories
Sarkar wears sunglasses with UV protection, and when outdoors for longer periods a broad-brimmed hat, scarf or dupatta(long, shawl-like cloth), and she carries an umbrella. Savvidou would love to carry a parasol, “but it’s windy on the Acropolis, and we lose them. Hats make you sweat, so we wear visors, because they protect your face from the sun, but your head is in the air.”
Duong and Van say battery-powered fans have taken off in Vietnamese cities but “people still use paper fans, and some use the traditional Vietnamese hat as a fan”. For Vallejo Carmona, her traditional hand fan “comes everywhere with me. It’s a very Sevillano thing.” She also opts for “light footwear, preferably made of leather, so the foot can be naked and fresh”.
Stop fantasising about air con
If you were guiltily Googling the cost of installing an air-conditioning unit mid-heatwave, Jayhas news for you: “There are many more sustainable ways to cool down. We have AC at home, but we haven’t turned it on in years. We installed ceiling fans, which work a treat. The more airflow you get across the skin the better, so if you’re lying on a bed, a ceiling fan is probably best; if you’re at a desk, a pedestal fan.” Salvo concurs: “When it’s very hot, I sleep with the fan on. I try to avoid the air con.”
Shutter up
You’ve heard all about closing the curtains, but here’s how it’s viewed where it has been a custom for generations. Salvo says: “In Italy, tradition has taught us to close the shutters during the day to keep the house dim and shield it from the sun, keeping it cooler. We then open the windows early in the morning and in the evening when the air cools down.”
Romel Bernal, an architect in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, where recent temperatures have reached 38C, has a nifty tip: “Blackout curtains help a room retain its temperature when not in use during the day, while light-coloured linen materials offer a cooling effect – and if you mist them with water, the evaporation keeps them cool.”
Get a thermometer
Schwandt recommendsinvesting ina thermometer “to get an objective measure of when it’s OK to open windows”. Jay agrees, saying, “We’ve installed a temperature sensor inside and another outside so we can look at the difference. That way, we can keep the windows open when it’s cooler outside than in, and when that flips, we shut the windows.”
Sit under a tree
As the climate heats up, nature can provide excellent relief. “The temperature on our forecast is measured in the shade, so if you’re out in the sun you’re exposed to 12 to 15 degrees higher heat load when you take into account the extra radiation,” says Jay. “Sitting under a tree is a nice way of getting shade. Grass also dampens the absorption of radiation, which is another moderating effect. Depending on the type of tree, you have the evapotranspiration effect, where water in the leaves evaporates and reduces ambient temperature by a couple more degrees celsius.” It’s why, says Haindongo, when the heat gets too much, “I lie under a tree, or climb to the hilltop for the breeze.”
… Or create shade with canopies and drapes
“You can achieve a microclimate in any home by taking advantage of natural resources, like plants and trees that create shade and absorb the impact of the heat. Landscape design has gone from being a luxury to being essential,” Bernal says. Vallejo Carmona describes how internal patios in many houses in Seville are “covered by thick fabric to create shade and coolness, and the council covers some streets with awnings to avoid the direct sun and create shade”.
Jay notes that while you can create shade in your garden, you must couple it with decent ventilation. “Some people create shade that blocks the prevailing wind, and then you get hot, because there’s no airflow.” Think sails or awnings, but choose heavy fabrics, as “some fabrics let radiation through because they’re not a tight enough weave,” he says.
Use mulch
Salvo says increasing temperatures are changing the way people garden. “Gardeners and farmers are increasingly using mulch to reduce evaporation. By practising this ancient method, we can increase soil water retention, protect roots from extreme heat and provide plants with more nutrients. We are also choosing more drought-resistant species, such as olive trees, lavender, rosemary, sage and Mediterranean native plants.”
Start ’em young
Australia has been incredibly successful at bringing skin cancer rates down among younger people, while here in the UK they are continuing to increase. It’s why starting some basic rules early is a great idea. “When Australian kids go to school, they have wide-brimmed hats and are not allowed to go out in the playground if they don’t have them on,” says Jay. “These very strong rules around sun safety start as early as five, and by the time you’re an adult, putting sunscreen on is like putting your underpants on – everybody does it every day.”
Stay safe in the water
Horribly, heatwaves are often coupled with drownings, so safety in the water is paramount. “Many people enter the sea unprepared after long periods in the sun, some after consuming alcohol, and end up ignoring the risks of currents, depth and sea conditions,” says Nascimento. “It’s important to respect lifeguard signals, swim in protected areas and never enter the sea alone. Extreme heat also increases physical strain on the body, so it’s necessary to recognise its limits.”
Almaitah says that “many people underestimate sun exposure because they feel cool in the water, but the combination of direct sunlight and reflection from the sea can cause severe sunburn, especially on boats, where exposure can be continuous”.
Socialise later
“We socialise as much as possible,” says Vallejo Carmona, “but during the hours of the worst heat, between 1pm and 6pm, most families are at home. After dinner, once it’s cool, neighbours gather with chairs to chat on the pavements outside, so by the time we go home to sleep, our houses are fresh.”
Duong and Van “sit out in the evenings to have trà đá, a traditional tea, but instead of having it hot in a cup, we dilute it in a big glass and put lots of ice in. It’s a lovely, traditional way of people having some cool air outdoors and socialising after a day of hiding from the heat.”
Slow your pace
“When I was doing my PhD, I did a field study in Seville in summer,” says Jay. “I immediately noticed that people moved more slowly and walked close to the side of a building to get shade.” Nascimento concurs: “Control your pace – it’s important to manage your energy throughout the day.” Almaitah says: “People often try to continue normal activities, but in very hot weather it’s important to slow down, stay hydrated, seek shade regularly and listen to the body’s warning signs.”
Moussa has similar advice – “We adapt by working early in the morning or later in the day, and prioritising essential tasks” – but says there’s another side to it: “We work in extreme conditions, yet every day we also see hundreds of migrants crossing this same desert with access to nothing: no water, no shoes, no shelter. Some of our energy comes precisely from that, from the drive to help someone who has less than you do.”
Lower your expectations of sleep
“The body naturally needs to cool slightly before sleep begins, so when temperatures remain above 40C, that becomes more difficult,” says El-Sioufi. “People often take longer to fall asleep, wake more frequently and spend less time in restorative deep sleep. Infants and young children are especially vulnerable, because their ability to regulate body temperature is less developed. Parents should be flexible and, rather than focusing on exact nap durations, ensure children remain hydrated, cool and comfortable.” Schwandt also says parents need “openness to changing schedules – because kids will go pretty close to flat out before they stop. Move playtimes to early morning and late evening, and recognise that oftentimes kids won’t fall asleep easily because of the heat, and that can transmit to fatigue the next day.”
Adapt your home
Rather than a total overhaul, Bernal recommends that you “reduce the impact of the heat in the areas of the home most used by its inhabitants”. Cross ventilation is crucial, so open windows and doors at opposite ends of your home and leave spaces clear to allow air to flow. “You can integrate technologies like windows with double and triple glazing, and windows with protective overhangs to minimise solar exposure. Outdoors, choose white for facades directly exposed to the sun and sand and beige tones for flooring, as they don’t cause glare or reflect heat.” Cement tiles, terracotta, light-coloured cantera stone and brushed-finish marble are excellent choices for preventing outside surfaces from overheating, and are suitable for walking barefoot.
And finally … splash about
Pacherrez Antón shares that “in Piura, during the summer, we have carnavales, where neighbours, tourists and the whole population gather, and water tanks and hoses are used to spray everyone as they dance and enjoy themselves”. Even if you are miles from Peru’s city of eternal heat, a local splash park or fountain should do the trick … just not at midday!

Britain braces for fourth heatwave of year as fire chiefs issue public appeal
Temperatures up to 35C forecast, triggering heat health alerts and pleas to take care in parched parks and rural areas
Paramedics and firefighters are braced for emergencies across the country this week after UK forecasters predicted a fourth heatwave of the year.
Temperatures are forecast to reach as high as 35C by Wednesday, triggering heat health alerts and an appeal from fire chiefs to take care in parched parks and rural areas.
July has been 3C above average across the UK, according to provisional Met Office data, and with more than a month of summer left, the UK has already faced more days above 30C than ever before.
Southern England has had just 1% of its average July rainfall, while England as a whole has had 5% and the UK 20%, according to the Met Office.
Forecasters predict this latest heatwave will at least be shortlived. Temperatures are expected to rise from Tuesday, reaching 30C as a high pressure system sits across the east and south-east of the country, before the peak of the heat comes on Wednesday.
Temperatures would begin to gradually cool from Thursday, the Met Office said, except in the south-east where another hot day could keep the region in official heatwave conditions.
The heat was likely to have a significant impact on the health of vulnerable people and increase demand on health services, the UK Health Security Agency said on Monday, as it issued amber heat health alerts for the east and south-east of England.
They begin on Wednesday at 9am and end on Thursday. Yellow heat health alerts will remain in place for Yorkshire and the Humber, West Midlands and south-west regions for the same time period.
Ambulance and emergency medical teams anticipate a surge in patients suffering dehydration, heat exhaustion and heatstroke, as well as from patients with heart and respiratory illnesses that can be badly exacerbated by high temperatures.
“Recent episodes of extreme heat have shown how quickly patients can become seriously unwell,” said Helen Vine, the assistant director of the Association of Ambulance Chief Executives (AACE).
“With amber heat health alerts in place, we would urge people to take the risks seriously by staying hydrated, avoiding strenuous activity during the hottest parts of the day, limiting alcohol consumption and seeking advice from NHS 111 for non-emergency health concerns.”
With wildfires across Europe displacing hundreds of thousands of people in France and Spain in recent days, UK fire chiefs were also priming themselves for the possibility that the latest heatwave could increase the chance of further wildfires in the UK.
Residents of Nethy Bridge in Scotland had to be evacuated at the weekend after a large fire broke out in the Cairngorms national park. And at the height of the third heatwave in mid-July, firefighters were battling 19 significant wildfires simultaneously in England and Wales.
On Monday a spokesperson for the National Fire Chiefs Council urged the public to avoid using disposable barbecues in parks, the countryside and other green spaces, and to take care with cigarette butts. “It only takes one spark to start a wildfire, and what may appear to be a small fire can quickly escalate, threatening communities, wildlife, natural habitats and the firefighters tackling the incident.”
Human-caused climate breakdown is making every heatwave in the world more intense and more likely to happen. The sustained increase in temperatures may lead to a redefinition of the criteria for a heatwave. Heatwave thresholds for some counties were nudged up by a degree four or five years ago, said the senior Met Office meteorologist Marco Petagna.
“Going forward they’ll need to be adjusted to take into account … current climate, otherwise we’re going to more frequently go into heatwaves. It’s a moveable thing, really, as we go through a warming world.”

France and Spain race to contain huge wildfires before fresh heatwave begins
Coming days are ‘absolutely critical’ for firefighters before temperatures rise again this week, officials say
Firefighters in France and Spain are racing to bring huge wildfires under control before another heatwave this week that will complicate efforts to tame the flames.
Spain’s interior minister, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, said Monday and Tuesday were “absolutely crucial days” before temperatures rise again from Wednesday, prompting prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, to warn: “We face difficult hours, complex hours” ahead.
EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year for the area of land burned.
A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares (125,000 acres). Authorities are battling two separate fires north-west of Madrid, taking the total area of scorched land near the capital to 70,000 hectares.
Spain’s state meteorological agency, Aemet, said the heatwave would last until “at least” Sunday, “making firefighting efforts more difficult due to high temperatures [and] locally gusty southerly winds”.
France was also in “a race against time” to control wildfires before another heatwave this week, said Eric Brocardi, a fire service spokesperson. Weather forecasters have said temperatures could reach 40C (104F) is some parts of the country from Tuesday.
This would complicate efforts to control the wildfire in Gironde in south-west France, which the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, described as “extremely intense and unpredictable … generating its own winds and advancing erratically toward the Bordeaux metropolitan area”.
The mayor of Bordeaux, Thomas Cazenave, told the BBC he is bracing for “all eventualities”, as the fire advanced to within 15km (nine miles) from the city. “We are preparing to accommodate a large number of people should further evacuations be ordered,” he said.
On a visit to Bordeaux, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, said: “The coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out.”
But he said a smaller fire in the adjoining Landes – which forced the evacuation of more than 30,000 people – was “contained” but remained “virulent”. “We must be extremely cautious over the next few hours and the coming days,” he said.
The Gironde fire has so far burned 42,000 hectares, making it one of the biggest devastations of land in France since the second world war.
In the Cestas commune, about 10 miles from the city of Bordeaux, firefighters used mechanical diggers to uproot trees in an attempt to create a firebreak.
The vast fire, which has triggered the evacuation of 220,000 people, had not progressed during the early hours of Monday but was “not contained” and remained “very complicated to control”, Nuñez said.
Speaking after an emergency meeting of the French government on Monday, he described this year’s wildfires as “completely exceptional”. More than 116,000 hectares of forest and vegetation have been burned since January, far exceeding the 70,000 hectares reported for the whole of 2025.
Spain’s government said the 172,000 hectares of forested land burned this year was six times greater than the equivalent figure for 2025.
Sánchez told a climate conference the wildfires were not isolated incidents.
“It is the most painful manifestation of a climate emergency that is making … wildfires more voracious and heatwaves more frequent, and as a result our land more vulnerable,” he said. “It is no longer an exception. It is the rule.”
The European Commission’s lead official on the green transition, Teresa Ribera, said Europe was not prepared for the consequences of the climate crisis. In an interview with El País she said the commission would propose an adaptation strategy in October that would be much more comprehensive than policies implemented so far.
A series of heatwaves, including record-breaking temperatures in June, that scientists say would have been impossible without the climate crisis, has left parched soils and tinder-dry vegetation that have fuelled this summer’s fires.
A European Commission official said the wildfire season had begun in April and could last until early November. Officials also stressed the rising risks for fighting wildfires from the middle of the week in France, Spain and Greece.
The EU executive has coordinated the dispatch of seven planes and four helicopters to France, as well as six planes and three forest firefighting teams to Spain, after the countries triggered the bloc’s emergency assistance mechanism. EU officials have also been sent to the Bordeaux region to assist local authorities.
Officials stressed the unprecedented nature of recent fires, which have spread rapidly over large areas. A commission official said that a recent fire in southern Spain that killed 13 people had reached speeds of 4 mph, while firefighters are able to react only to fires moving 300 metres an hour or less.
The scale of Europe’s wildfires has raised questions about the continent’s ability to respond. Italy is among about 10 European countries that have sent firefighting equipment or teams to France and Spain while grappling with its own blazes.
Several fires broke out in northern and central Portugal, officials said, with over 1,000 firefighters and other professionals battling the flames.
Firefighters fought to extinguish a major wildfire in Italy’s southern region of Puglia on Monday. More than 400 people, many of them tourists staying in campsites set among pine forests, were evacuated by sea from the Gargano peninsula on Sunday as the blaze, fanned by strong winds, encroached on beaches.
A further 58 people were evacuated from their homes in Maratea as a wildfire swept through neighbouring Basilicata.
Italy is bracing for its fourth heatwave this year as temperatures edge up towards highs of 38C to 40C from Wednesday.
Smoke from the fires in France is continuing to cause a “marked deterioration” in air quality across a swathe of the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region and beyond, with health authorities warning about the danger.
Elderly people, pregnant women and those with respiratory issues and chronic conditions were advised to take precautions. Local health authorities said people should close windows, wear an FFP2 mask outside and avoid strenuous activity.
The prime minister’s office said more than 1.5 million FFP2 masks had been sent to the region.

NAVALUENGA (SPAIN) - Spain has two crucial days in front of it to bring wildfires under control before weather conditions worsen, authorities said Monday, as Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez called on citizens to "exercise extreme caution" ahead of a new heatwave.
Wildfires that broke out in forests around the Spanish capital at the height of the summer holidays have forced some 60,000 people to flee their homes, often with just minutes' notice, some leaving pets and medicine behind.
"You run to save what you can and then you turn to defend" against the fire, said Karim Benali, 39, a volunteer who spoke to AFP on a road near Navaluenga, west of Madrid.
"There were some 48 homes here, they burned," he said, surrounded by charred earth and trees blanketed with a persistent smell of smoke.
The fires devoured forests left tinder-dry by successive heatwaves and lack of rain since May.
David Sanchez, a 48-year-old painter and decorator, had just returned home to Cebreros after evacuating at the weekend to find that his small olive and pistachio grove had been consumed by the inferno.
"Now it's time to clean up and plant again and that's it. It's crap, to be honest. And the fire has flared up again down there," he said, surrounded by air still smokey enough to burn the eyes and throat.
Overnight, lower temperatures, weaker winds and higher air humidity helped make progress against the blazes west of the capital, the Madrid regional government said.
"The situation has improved slightly, but the fire is still active," it said.
But with humidity levels about to drop and temperatures soar across Spain, hitting 42C in the northeast and 39C in the centre according to meteorological agency AEMET, firefighters have only a small window of opportunity.
- 'Extreme caution' -
Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska told reporters that Monday and Tuesday "are absolutely decisive days" to control the fires, before temperatures start rising again.
"The next two days will not bring the most favourable conditions, nor the ones we would have wanted, but they are two days in which we can take the initiative, make progress, and work towards controlling and containing the blaze."
AEMET officially declared that a heatwave, the fourth of the summer, would begin on Tuesday, lasting until "at least" Sunday.
"The wildfire danger level will continue to increase, reaching extreme levels and making firefighting efforts more difficult due to high temperatures, locally gusty southerly winds and widespread low humidity," it said in a statement.
Reacting to the forecast, Sanchez said: "I ask for understanding and call on all citizens in all the country to exercise extreme caution and take every possible precaution."
"We face difficult hours, complex hours" ahead, he warned.
- 'Lost everything' -
In Chapineria, west of Madrid, the flames had torn through dozens of vehicles at an industrial park, leaving charred shells behind, AFP photographers saw.
Meanwhile, at a sports hall in Las Rozas de Madrid just outside the capital, the displaced sprawled on camp beds, held their heads in their hands and comforted pets as they awaited news.
Maria Angeles Canete fought back tears as she looked around the desolation that used to be her campsite near Navaluenga.
"We lost everything," she said, of the site that used to draw a wide range of international tourists. "We had this campsite, we had another one, and we've lost it all. We have nothing."
Scientists say climate change is making extreme weather events more frequent and intense.
Sanchez blamed global warming on Monday, describing the fires as "the most painful expression of a climate emergency".
"This is no longer an exception, this is a rule itself," he added during a meeting in Madrid.
Sanchez was due to visit a fire-hit area in Valencia, in the east of the country where firefighters are battling a separate blaze and 15,000 more people have been evacuated.
The fires in the Iberian country have affected an area of 77,000 hectares (190,000 acres) -- nearly the size of New York City -- according to the authorities.
Since the start of the year, fires in Spain have ravaged 150,000 hectares and killed 13 people, according to Sanchez.

It’s a sweet little town, Arcachon. Clinging to the long French Atlantic coast, adorned with Victorian villas and pretty flowerbeds, it reminds me oddly of the English town of Bournemouth. By which I mean: Bournemouth before it was ruined. As such, it’s the kind of place that usually calls for a return visit. I am sure for many French people it is a holiday regular – “ahh, shall we do Arcachon again? Mais oui, we can try that new oyster cabin.” But right now I seriously wonder if anyone will want to return to Arcachon, ever.
The reasons are twofold. Firstly, the news is full of searing images: of people fleeing the wildfires on Cap Ferret, and being ferried, like wartime evacuees, across the bay to Arcachon after a summer of repeated heatwaves. Secondly, several weeks ago I personally experienced the worst of those heatwaves, in and around Arcachon, and it changed my mind about the emotional impact of climate change.
My torrid holiday from hell began in green, bucolic Aveyron, where I was on assignment. Everything was so pleasant and as the official trip came to an end I thought: why not extend the adventure? My calendar was empty, I already had a hired car and I was keen to explore a part of France I’ve never seen before – the French Atlantic coast between Brittany and Bayonne.
The only fly in the ointment was the weather forecast. When I turned to my sensible AI – NinaGPT – to construct a coastal itinerary, she kept saying “Are you sure you want to do this Sean, there is a heatwave coming.” I scolded her for being a nanny and laughingly reminded her I’m a travel veteran; I like hot sunny weather and I’ve been to several war zones. I set off.
Major mistake. One afternoon, parked by an Aldi west of Conques, I watched with grim amazement as the thermometer in my car registered the intensifying heat: 116F, 118F, 120F. I actually took photographs. It was surely not that hot in reality: car thermometers are unreliable, especially if you’re sitting on baked tarmac. Nonetheless it was indicative of the heat dome settling over France. It also reminded me of the last time I’d stared at a car thermometer in wary amazement. That was in the Fish River Canyon in southern Namibia. That time, my car told me it was 115F. I took a photograph then, as well.
By the time I reached sun-struck Moissac the heatwave was near its raging peak. I quickly learned the French for this phenomenon: canicule. I also learned the sobering truth that much of provincial France lacks air conditioning. Its buildings rely on shutters, thick walls and ventilation; defenses which begin to fail above 95F. In the main square of Moissac I scurried to a shady but uncooled brasserie to bash out an article. The sweat dripped from my nose onto my laptop. Then I watched TV, as President Macron warned that the “hottest day in French history” was approaching.
It came as I arrived in Arcachon. I’d booked an apartment, right on the beach, which looked suitably modern. I figured sea breezes plus air conditioning would see me through the worst. As I pulled up, around 6pm, it was a brutal, stifling 102F. There was no sea breeze. The sea in the bay looked sad and listless, repressed by a despotic sun. To top it all off, even here there was no air conditioning.
I hadn’t checked the small print. Stupidly I’d just assumed the flat would be properly kitted out, because it was so clearly brand new. Not only did it have no air conditioning, but it also had no fans and no through breeze. It was maybe 122F in the punishment block of the bedroom. My reservation was non-refundable but I kicked up such a fuss on Booking.com’s helpline – “I could die in there” (I wasn’t joking) – they agreed to a refund. I used the money to find a grand hotel with climatisation. And then I hid.
Because that is all you can do when the thermometer soars over 104F. Hide. Shelter in place. It is like sitting out an air raid, or a hurricane, except it goes on for longer. Every time I did venture out, I got an instant pounding headache and I hurried back inside.
It was a truly horrible experience, and I write as someone who has been through severe heat. I’ve been in Luxor, Egypt when it hit 109F, I’ve been in Death Valley, Eastern California during similar. Somehow, they were more tolerable than Arcachon, France during the recent canicule. Perhaps because you expect great heat in deserts but not in the suburbs of Bordeaux; perhaps because the proximity of the sea added humidity.
I’ve had just one experience which compares to what happened in France, in the Danakil Depression, Ethiopia. I arrived at dusk in a village of mud huts, ready to climb the famous, lava-lake volcano of Erta Ale. There it was about 108F at 6pm – similar to southwest France, recently. But it’s not just the temperature that echoed: in both places I had the sensation of being trapped and tormented. Of suffering inescapably. And the mud huts had no air conditioning.
The obvious question arises. If these heatwaves continue, and worsen, what will they do to Europe, and European life? No one can be certain, but I remember my charming, capricious Auntie Lois, who spent her life shifting nervously around the world. At one point she fled Los Angeles after an earthquake. At the time I put it down to her highly-strung nature; an over-reaction. And yet I now think of her explanation, “The earthquake changed the way I felt about California. I felt like my home was turning on me, that the ground beneath me couldn’t be trusted.”
Perhaps Europe will be fine, we will briskly adapt – and install air conditioning everywhere. That’s what I used to believe. But now I am not sure. Maybe we will react like Lois, and we will lose trust in the skies. Perhaps millions will avoid southern Europe. Certainly, there are only so many times you can experience an earthquake before you think – that’s it, I’m out of here, and I’m not coming back. Especially not for summer holidays. As for my auntie Lois, she ended up living in Scotland.

The India Meteorological Department (IMD) issued a ‘yellow’ alert for Delhi as rain lashed several parts of the national capital on Monday evening. The weather agency has predicted similar conditions to persist across several Delhi districts until late evening.
Rainfall and cloudy skies across Jantar Mantar and Kartavya Path brought welcome relief from the humidity, though the showers triggered traffic slowdowns for commuters in multiple areas.
Light rain and light thunderstorms accompanied by lightning and gusty winds with speeds of 30-40 kmph are very likely, according to the IMD's district-level nowcast issued at 4:24 pm.
The alert is in place over parts of South East Delhi, East Delhi, Shahdara, Central Delhi, North East Delhi, South Delhi, New Delhi, South West Delhi, West Delhi, North West Delhi and North Delhi.
The weather office did not issue any warning for the remaining districts.
26.6 degrees Celsius with 98 per cent relative humidity on Monday morning, the Met Dept said, noting that Northeasterly winds were blowing at around 9 kmph.
Temperatures at the Safdarjung base station are forecast to peak at 36°C, with the minimum settling around 27°C.
The IMD expects rainfall across the National Capital Region (NCR) to be highly localised. This means residents might see short, intense downpours in certain neighbourhoods, while other areas could remain completely dry.
Despite recent spells of rain, Delhi is grappling with a 14% moisture deficit for the season. Between June 1 and July 25, the capital recorded 247.8 mm of rain—well below the typical 365.3 mm. However, the IMD continues to officially classify the city's monsoon performance as “normal”.
Uttar Pradesh is bracing for intensified monsoon activity that promises relief from the region's stifling humidity over the next few days. The Regional Meteorological Centre in Lucknow expects widespread rain, thunderstorms, and lightning to sweep across the state.
The forecast indicates that most of eastern UP and many parts of western UP will experience thunderstorms on Monday, with the weather system expanding further across the state on Tuesday and Wednesday.
The IMD has issued warnings for isolated thunderstorms and lightning through July 30. While Monday will see heavy rain in isolated pockets, residents should prepare for heavy to very heavy rainfall on Tuesday and Wednesday.
